'''Harriet Redfield Cobb''' (September 10, 1866 – February 13, 1958) was an American mathematics educator, a professor at [[Smith College]] from 1895 to 1931.

== Early life and education ==
Cobb was born in [[Peekskill, New York]], the daughter of Elisha G. Cobb and Esther Meroa Redfield Cobb. Her father was a Congregational clergyman. She attended Northampton High School and earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics at Smith College in 1889, and an honorary master's degree, also from Smith College, in 1891.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1891-06-25|title=Young Women Get Degrees at Smith|pages=2|work=New-York Tribune|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86895069/young-women-get-degrees-at-smith/|access-date=2021-10-11|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She pursued further studies at [[Columbia University]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Leonard|first=John William|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GvwUAAAAYAAJ&q=Redfield&pg=PA188|title=Woman's Who's who of America: A Biographical Dictionary of Contemporary Women of the United States and Canada, 1914-1915|date=1914|publisher=American Commonwealth Company|pages=187–188|language=en}}</ref>

== Career ==
Cobb taught mathematics at schools in Louisiana and Ohio before returning to Smith as a mathematics instructor in 1895.<ref name=":0" /> She taught geometry<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last1=Beery|first1=Janet L.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eDVBDwAAQBAJ&dq=Harriet+Redfield+Cobb&pg=PA310|title=Women in Mathematics: Celebrating the Centennial of the Mathematical Association of America|last2=Greenwald|first2=Sarah J.|last3=Jensen-Vallin|first3=Jacqueline A.|last4=Mast|first4=Maura B.|date=2017-12-02|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-319-66694-5|pages=310, 315|language=en}}</ref> at Smith College<ref>{{Cite book|last=Green|first=Judy|title=Pioneering women in American mathematics : the pre-1940 PhD's|date=2009|publisher=American Mathematical Society|others=Jeanne LaDuke|isbn=978-1-4704-1839-7|location=Providence, R.I.|page=27|oclc=989866060}}</ref> until she retired as professor emerita in 1931. Her colleagues at Smith included fellow mathematics professors [[Eleanor P. Cushing]]. [[Ruth Goulding Wood]], and [[Suzan Rose Benedict]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6TtJAQAAMAAJ&dq=Harriet+Redfield+Cobb&pg=RA1-PA73|title=Official Circular of Smith College|date=1906|publisher=Smith College|pages=73|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Smith College|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aD_PAAAAMAAJ&dq=Harriet+Redfield+Cobb&pg=PA64|title=Bulletin|date=1924|publisher=|pages=64|language=en}}</ref> She was a member of [[Phi Beta Kappa]] and a president of the Western Massachusetts Mathematics Association. She also taught Bible study classes at a Congregational church.<ref name=":0" />

Cobb was a busy traveler. She made an eight-month trip around the world with her friend, Pennsylvania math educator Sarah Gilbert, in 1907 and 1908.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1921-02-07|title=Retires after Long Service|pages=11|work=Lancaster New Era|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86895294/retires-after-long-service/|access-date=2021-10-11|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She traveled to China several times in the 1920s,<ref>{{Cite news|date=1928-03-08|title=Ecuador Due Today with 100 Passengers|pages=11|work=News-Pilot|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86895001/ecuador-due-today-with-100-passengers/|access-date=2021-10-11|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> and consulted there on math education for Chinese women.<ref name=":1" />

Cobb spent much of her retirement in Florida.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1941-01-25|title=Knitting for Bundles for Britain|pages=11|work=Tampa Bay Times|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86894641/knitting-for-bundles-for-britain/|access-date=2021-10-11|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She was active in Smith alumnae activities there.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1938-02-05|title=Smith Alumnae Entertained|pages=12|work=Tampa Bay Times|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86894825/smith-alumnae-entertained/|access-date=2021-10-11|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> In 1936 she spoke to an audience of retired teachers in Florida about "The Pioneer Spirit of Smith College".<ref>{{Cite news|date=1936-12-04|title=Miss Harriet R. Cobb to Address Teachers|pages=8|work=Tampa Bay Times|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86894501/miss-harriet-r-cobb-to-address-teachers/|access-date=2021-10-11|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Cobb died in 1958, aged 91 years, in [[Northampton, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{Cite news|date=1958-02-14|title=Obituary for Harriet Redfield Cobb (Aged 91)|pages=26|work=The Boston Globe|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86876105/obituary-for-harriet-redfield-cobb/|access-date=2021-10-11|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>
